d.title: 2.62 MB per token on the wire, and what the link does to it
d.caption: Tensor parallelism all-reduces a vector of `hidden_size` after the attention block and again after the feed-forward one — on Llama-2 70B that is **2 × 80 × 8192 × 2 bytes = 2.62 MB per token**. The ceiling that imposes is the right-hand column, and the spread is the architectural decision: NVLink 4 puts the ceiling far above anything a model can produce, while **100 GbE caps you at 4,768 tokens/sec** before the model does any work.

d.title: Decode is latency-bound on the wire; prefill is bandwidth-bound
d.caption: The payload is `hidden_size` per **token**, and decode has one token per request — so the message is a few kilobytes, firmly in the latency-dominated regime. At batch 1 the fixed per-message cost is **251× the bandwidth term on NVLink 4**, which means a faster link buys nothing for decode and a lower-latency one buys everything. Prefill sends hundreds of tokens at once and inverts it. This is why a serving cluster and a training cluster want different interconnects.

d.title: The pipeline bubble, and why decode is the worst case for it
d.caption: A P-stage pipeline idles for `(P−1)/(M+P−1)` of its device-time, where M is the work in flight. In training M is the micro-batch count and can be large, so the bubble shrinks to 1.5% at 2 stages. **In decode there is one token in flight per step, so M = 1** — and the bubble is (P−1)/P: 50% at two stages, **87.5% at eight**. Which is the whole reason pipeline parallelism is a training technique that serving uses only when the model will not fit any other way.

d.title: The all-to-all nobody can size in advance
d.caption: An MoE layer with 8 experts activating 2 per token cuts compute per token by 4× against a dense layer of the same width — that is the point of the architecture. Putting experts on different devices introduces an **all-to-all**: every token must reach the devices holding its chosen experts and the results must come back. Unlike tensor parallelism's all-reduce, **the volume is not fixed in advance** — it depends on how the router assigned this particular batch, so a skewed batch produces a hot device and the whole step waits for it.

d.title: Magnitude pruning: quality destroyed, speed unchanged
d.caption: The intuition is sound — most weights in a trained network are small and contribute little — and the intuition about *speed* is simply wrong. At 50% sparsity perplexity goes from 5.941 to **3048, a factor of 513**, and the forward pass gets **no faster at all**: 622.4 ms against a 662.2 ms baseline, which is noise. Zeros in a dense tensor are still multiplied, so unstructured pruning buys nothing without hardware or kernels that exploit the pattern. Note also the non-monotonicity at 90%, where perplexity *improves* relative to 70% — both numbers mean the model is broken.

d.title: DistilBERT delivers the size and speed, and disagrees on the answers
d.caption: 61.2% of the parameters, 6 layers of 12, and **2.01× the speed** — the compression claims hold exactly. What the probes show is the part a size table cannot: on top-1 masked-token prediction the two models **disagree**, with BERT answering *paris* where DistilBERT answers *marseille*. The extra signal distillation captures is real — a teacher putting 0.6 on "cat" and 0.3 on "dog" tells the student dogs are nearly cats, which a one-hot label cannot — and it is still a smaller model that knows less.

d.title: Which of the three, and the fourth option people skip
d.caption: Quantization is nearly always the right **first** answer, because it needs no retraining and composes with everything else. Distillation is the only one of the three that can *beat* the original on your own distribution, because the student is trained on your data. And the last row is the honest one that gets skipped: **a smaller off-the-shelf model that passes your evaluation is strictly better than compressing a larger one**, because somebody else paid for the training.

d.title: Five routing signals, and what each actually predicts
d.caption: Because the price spread across models is large — 3.12 measures **23×** across one provider's list — even a mediocre router pays for itself. The arithmetic that matters is not accuracy but the cost of the two error types: a hard request sent to the small model produces a bad answer or a retry, while an easy request sent to the large one costs money and nothing else. **So bias toward the large model.** The last row is the trap: asking the big model to triage spends exactly what you were trying to save.

d.title: Four numbers, and what each one hides
d.caption: Measured with a real scheduling loop rather than a formula — 24 Poisson arrivals, fixed slots, a real prefill per admission and a real decode step per active row. The hiding is the point: **TTFT at low load is mostly prefill and under load is mostly queueing**, which is the single most misread thing about it. TPOT is a *distribution*, not a number — mean 124.0 ms against a p99 of 432.5 and a max of 678.5. And queue depth is the only one of the four that is a leading indicator.

d.title: Three definitions of throughput, differing by 3.4x
d.caption: Total tokens over wall clock tells you what the system can **produce**; the rate a single stream experiences tells you what a user **feels**. On the same run those are 12.6 and 3.7 tokens per second, because four streams shared the device so each received roughly a quarter of the output. Both get called throughput. **A capacity plan built on the per-user figure under-provisions by 3.4×**, and a user-experience claim built on the capacity figure is off by the same factor in the other direction.

d.title: The same p99, aggregated three ways, differing by 2.8x
d.caption: TPOT is a distribution over gaps, and gaps are **grouped inside requests** — so "the p99 TPOT" is ambiguous. Pooling every gap gives 1120.9 ms; taking each request's p99 and averaging gives 702.9; taking each request's *mean* and then percentiles gives 404.8. All three get called p99 TPOT and the spread is **2.8×**. The tail explains why: the worst 1% of gaps belong to just 3 of 24 requests, so pooling counts one bad request many times and per-request averaging counts it once.

d.title: The sweep, including the result that goes the wrong way
d.caption: A load test should produce a curve, not a number: hold the arrival pattern fixed, vary the concurrency limit, read throughput and the percentiles **together**. On this 4-thread CPU more slots made everything worse — throughput falls from 31.3 to 12.1 tok/s while p50 TPOT rises 18× — because the arithmetic saturates immediately and extra concurrency only adds contention. On a GPU the first few rows would climb. The transferable part is the method: the optimum is where throughput stops rising **before** the percentiles break, and that point is a property of your hardware, not a recommended setting.

d.title: Four signals, and why these four
d.caption: Queue depth is first because it is **the only leading indicator** — it rises before any latency does, which makes it the right thing to autoscale on. TTFT p99 should be read as queueing rather than as model speed: **64–99% of it was queue** in this measurement. And KV cache utilisation is the one nobody watches: preemption and recompute start around 90% and are invisible in the latency right up until they are not.
